quick: Induction 0.15 mg/kg/day IV until remission; then consolidation 0.15 mg/kg/day
Do not breastfeed during and after therapy
Avoid; no benefit and may add toxicity
ECG/QTc, electrolytes (K, Mg, Ca), CBC, differentiation syndrome
summary: Arsenic trioxide is an intravenous differentiating/cytotoxic agent for acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL). It carries boxed warnings for APL differentiation syndrome (which can be fatal) and for QT/QTc prolongation with torsades de pointes and complete AV block. Aggressive electrolyte and ECG monitoring and prompt corticosteroid treatment of differentiation syndrome are essential.
indications: Induction of remission and consolidation in adults with relapsed or refractory acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) characterized by t(15;17) or PML/RAR-alpha
First-line treatment of low-to-intermediate risk APL in combination with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA), where labeled/established

dosage.d: 0.15 mg/kg IV once daily until bone marrow remission (maximum 60 doses)
dosage.n: Infuse over 1-2 hours (up to 4 h if vasomotor reactions)

dosage.d: 0.15 mg/kg IV once daily, 5 days/week, for up to 25 doses over 5 weeks

admin: Dilute in 100-250 mL of 5% dextrose or 0.9% sodium chloride and infuse intravenously over 1-2 hours
Do not mix with other medications in the same infusion
Obtain baseline 12-lead ECG, electrolytes and creatinine before therapy
Maintain potassium >4 mEq/L and magnesium >1.8 mg/dL throughout treatment
Discontinue QT-prolonging drugs where possible before starting
moa: Arsenic trioxide causes degradation of the PML/RAR-alpha fusion oncoprotein, inducing partial differentiation and apoptosis of malignant promyelocytes. It triggers DNA fragmentation, alters mitochondrial membrane potential, generates reactive oxygen species and inhibits proliferation of APL cells.

relative: Baseline QTc prolongation or congenital long QT syndrome
monitor: History of arrhythmia or heart failure

preg: Can cause fetal harm; arsenic is teratogenic and embryotoxic. Contraindicated in pregnancy. Women and men of reproductive potential should use effective contraception during and for a period after treatment.
lact: Arsenic is excreted in human milk; do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 2 weeks after the final dose.
renal: Arsenic is primarily renally eliminated; use caution and monitor closely in renal impairment, and consider dose reduction in severe impairment.
hepatic: Use with caution and monitor liver function in hepatic impairment; hepatotoxicity has been reported.

major: Other QT-prolonging drugs (antiarrhythmics, certain antipsychotics, fluoroquinolones, azoles, ondansetron) - additive risk of torsades de pointes
Drugs causing electrolyte disturbance (diuretics, amphotericin) - potentiate QT risk
moderate: Drugs causing hepatotoxicity - additive liver injury
minor: Agents affecting renal clearance - altered arsenic elimination
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; no therapeutic relevance and may worsen toxicity.
interactions.diagnostics: Prolongs QT/QTc on ECG; causes leukocytosis and electrolyte shifts.

serious: QT/QTc prolongation and torsades de pointes
emergency: Differentiation syndrome (dyspnea, fever, pulmonary infiltrates, weight gain, effusions)
Torsades de pointes / sustained ventricular arrhythmia

monitoring: 12-lead ECG with QTc at baseline and at least weekly (more often if abnormal)
Serum potassium, magnesium and calcium at least twice weekly; keep K >4 and Mg >1.8
Complete blood count and coagulation profile frequently
Daily assessment for signs of differentiation syndrome (respiratory distress, fever, weight gain)
counsel: You will have frequent heart tracings (ECG) and blood tests for salts and blood counts
Report shortness of breath, fever, rapid weight gain or leg swelling immediately - signs of a serious lung reaction
Report palpitations, fainting or dizziness (heart rhythm effects)
Avoid other medicines that affect heart rhythm unless approved by your oncologist
Use effective contraception; do not breastfeed during treatment
pk: Differentiation effect over days to weeks
Trivalent arsenic terminal half-life approximately 10-14 hours
Tissue accumulation; effect over treatment course
Store ampoules at 20-25 C; use diluted solution promptly (refrigerate up to 24 h)
pearls: BOXED WARNING: APL differentiation syndrome - treat promptly with high-dose corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone) at first signs; do not necessarily stop arsenic
BOXED WARNING: QT prolongation, torsades de pointes and complete AV block - monitor ECG and aggressively correct potassium and magnesium
Keep serum potassium above 4 mEq/L and magnesium above 1.8 mg/dL throughout therapy
ATRA plus arsenic trioxide is highly effective and chemotherapy-sparing in low/intermediate-risk APL
Manage marked leukocytosis (often without cytotoxic chemotherapy) per protocol
missed: Doses are administered in a supervised oncology setting on a defined schedule; a missed or delayed dose is managed by the treating hematology-oncology team, not self-administered.
overdose: Symptoms of acute arsenic toxicity include convulsions, muscle weakness and confusion. Discontinue the drug and consider chelation therapy (e.g., dimercaprol/BAL, then penicillamine or DMSA) with supportive care and cardiac/electrolyte monitoring.
